strengths: Well-motivated activation-space steering approach with clear articulation of advantages over retraining/per-step optimization
Comprehensive methodological extensions including layer pruning (top-K, exponential weighting), time-based scheduling, and multi-direction steering with supporting ablations
Extensive experimental evaluation spanning probe classification, quantitative metrics, listening tests, temporal control analysis, and real-music transfer
Technically sound methodology with clear presentation and open science commitment (code release)
Practical engineering contributions that address domain-specific challenges of audio-domain steering
weaknesses: Limited core novelty—primarily adapts existing RFM method from Beaglehole et al. (2025b) with incremental engineering improvements; insufficient contribution for top-tier venue
Critical missing comparison to other controllable music generation methods (ControlNet, DITTO, finetuning baselines); cannot assess relative merit

Fundamental limitation: method works well only for notes (0.82 accuracy) but fails on abstract concepts (progressions: 0.11, intervals: 0.22, time signatures: 0.25); mean-pooling temporal modeling weakness acknowledged but unresolved

Severe control-quality trade-offs: Table 2 shows FD/MMD increase substantially with control strength; multi-direction steering causes CLAP to drop from ~0.32 to 0.13, undermining prompt adherence and practical applicability

Problematic evaluation relying on circular validation with SYNTHEORY-trained probes; limited real-music evaluation; small listening test (12 participants) with overlapping confidence intervals and no significance testing
Multi-direction steering results suggest fundamental limitations (strong constraint → text-adherence loss) without proposed solutions, severely limiting practical scenarios
Limited temporal control analysis: Section 6.2 evaluates schedules only on notes; unclear if time-varying steering works for other concepts; no evidence of temporal dynamics in generated sequences

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation including quantitative metrics, ablations, human studies on both synthetic and real data (SYNTHEORY and MusicBench)
Practical and well-motivated contribution: enables fine-grained control over frozen models without retraining or per-step optimization, addressing real limitations of existing methods
Meaningful engineering improvements demonstrated through ablations (layer pruning strategies, injection probability scheduling) that substantially improve generation quality while maintaining control
Strong targeted results on specific attributes (notes: 0.23→0.82 probe accuracy) with preserved text alignment (CLAP within 0.02 of baseline), demonstrating effective steering on primary use cases
Clear presentation with extensive methodological details, hyperparameter search spaces, ablations, and promised code release supporting reproducibility
Novel application domain: first adaptation of RFMs to music generation with layer-based and temporal control extensions
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: primarily applies existing RFM techniques (Radhakrishnan et al. 2023; Beaglehole et al. 2025b) with relatively straightforward engineering extensions; no significant methodological innovations or music-specific insights

Heavy reliance on synthetic training data (SYNTHEORY) with acknowledged failures to generalize to real music; probes show poor transfer (e.g., tempo MSE 0.862 on MusicBench) undermining control claims

Severe domain-specificity: effectively controls only notes (0.23→0.82) but dramatically fails on complex/temporal attributes (progressions 0.07→0.11, time signatures 0.17→0.25, tempo unmeasured), contradicting 'fine-grained control' claims
Critical unresolved limitation: mean pooling discards temporal ordering acknowledged as root cause of failures on progressions/time signatures/scales—core musical properties deferred to future work

Significant quality-control trade-offs: multi-direction steering degrades CLAP by 37% (0.207 vs 0.332 baseline); stronger steering increases distribution shift (FD/MMD); no principled framework for hyperparameter selection

Major missing comparisons: no evaluation against other activation-steering methods (ACTADD, CAA) or recent controllable music generation approaches (ControlNet, DITTO), preventing assessment of relative performance

Probe-based evaluation reliability: RFM probes trained on synthetic data; paper explicitly disclaims accuracy interpretability ('should not be over-interpreted,' 'relative trends not ground-truth'), undermining main quantitative evidence
Limited human evaluation: only 12 participants on 4/7 attributes; mixed results and modest improvements on most attributes (chords 59.71→73.46, intervals 54.75→70.33)

strengths: Well-motivated application addressing practical problem of controllable music generation without retraining or per-step optimization
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including multiple metrics (FD, MMD, CLAP, probe accuracy), ablations, listening tests, and evaluation on both synthetic and real data
Thoughtful domain adaptation with layer pruning and stochastic gating specifically designed to address differences between text and audio steering
Clear empirical results on simpler concepts (notes reach 0.82 accuracy while maintaining ~0.02 CLAP degradation) with well-visualized control-fidelity trade-offs
Strong experimental rigor with detailed hyperparameter tuning, ablation studies, and promised code release supporting reproducibility
Insights like mean-pooling superiority over last-token pooling for capturing temporal structure are well-demonstrated
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution is straightforward application of existing RFMs; layer pruning, Bernoulli gating, and time schedules are standard engineering choices rather than novel methods

Heavy reliance on synthetic data with poor generalization: MusicBench results significantly worse than SYNTHEORY (75.3% vs 85% on notes; 67.5% vs 98.9% on keys), raising serious questions about real-world applicability

Severe limitations on sequential/complex musical attributes: mean-pooling discards temporal ordering; scales, progressions, time signatures underperform; these are precisely the musically important attributes
Circular evaluation metric: primary accuracy metrics use RFM probes trained on SYNTHEORY to evaluate SYNTHEORY-trained probes; acknowledged gap to real-world performance undermines claimed accuracies

Critical missing baselines: no comparison to other controllable generation methods (ControlNet, DITTO, LILAC, SMITIN) or simpler steering approaches (linear probes, PCA); impossible to assess relative merit of RFM approach

Inadequately addressed control-fidelity trade-offs: FD increases substantially at high control strengths; multi-direction steering severely degrades CLAP (0.33→0.17 for chords); unclear if this is true degradation or sampling artifacts
Limited experimental scope: only MUSICGEN-Large tested; only symbolic concepts addressed; listening test with 12 participants is modest; no computational cost analysis for probe training
Unclear methodological justification: why only top eigenvector; why Bernoulli gating; why RFMs better than simpler alternatives not demonstrated

strengths: Well-motivated adaptation of RFMs to music generation with domain-specific innovations (layer pruning, temporal schedules, multi-direction control) that go beyond simply applying existing methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple metrics (FD, MMD, CLAP, probe accuracy, external metrics), ablation studies, listening tests, and both synthetic and real-world validation
Practical contribution: no model finetuning required, lightweight probe training, inference-time steering without per-step optimization
Significant improvements in controllability demonstrated (e.g., note accuracy 0.23→0.82) while maintaining reasonable prompt adherence (CLAP within ~0.02 of baseline)
Thorough and honest presentation with clear methodology, extensive appendices, and acknowledged limitations
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily applies existing RFM framework (Radhakrishnan et al. 2023, Beaglehole et al. 2025b) with relatively straightforward domain-specific extensions rather than fundamental innovations

Critical evaluation limitation: RFM probes trained on synthetic SYNTHEORY data used to evaluate natural MusicGen outputs; authors acknowledge these should be 'relative indicators rather than absolute ground truth,' undermining confidence in main results

No comparison to other recent controllable music generation methods (Facchiano et al. 2025, Baker & Nistal 2025, Koo et al. 2025); only baseline is weak prompt-only conditioning, making it impossible to assess state-of-the-art performance

Quality-control trade-off more severe than presented: CLAP degrades 22% at highest η₀ for notes; multi-direction steering shows catastrophic CLAP degradation (0.318→0.167 for chords), questioning practical utility

Fundamental limitation with temporal modeling: mean-pooling discards temporal order, limiting performance on sequential music-theoretic concepts (scales, progressions, time signatures); acknowledged but not addressed
Weak performance on important concepts: tempo difficult to control (MSE=0.862 on MusicBench; Spearman ρ=0.283-0.433 with external metrics); progressions/scales underperform
Small listening test (12 participants, 24 samples) lacks statistical power; MusicBench evaluation preliminary with limited sample sizes
Hyperparameter complexity and sensitivity: multiple tunable parameters (η₀, w₀, κ, injection probability p) with unclear selection guidance; different concepts require different settings
Limited scope: only tested on MusicGen-Large; unclear generalization to other architectures; only music-theoretic concepts evaluated, not perceptual attributes
